text: Richard Evelyn Byrd Jr. (October 25, 1888 – March 11, 1957) was an American naval officer, pioneering aviator, polar explorer, and organizer of polar logistics. He served as a navigator and expedition leader in aircraft flights that crossed the Atlantic Ocean, a segment of the Arctic Ocean, and a segment of the Antarctic Plateau. He is credited with discovering Mount Sidley, the largest dormant volcano in Antarctica. Byrd claimed to be the first to reach both the North and South Poles by air, though there is controversy over whether he actually reached the North Pole, with some evidence suggesting the distance he claimed to have flown exceeded the possible fuel range of his aircraft. He received the Medal of Honor, the highest military decoration in the U.S. Armed Forces, and the Navy Cross, the second-highest honor for valor in the U.S. Navy. Born in Winchester, Virginia, to Esther Bolling (Flood) and Richard Evelyn Byrd Sr., he was a descendant of the First Families of Virginia, including John Rolfe, Pocahontas, William Byrd II, William Byrd I, Robert "King" Carter, George Yeardley, Francis Wyatt, and Samuel Argall. He was the brother of Virginia Governor and U.S. Senator Harry F. Byrd, whose father served as Speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates. On January 20, 1915, Byrd married Marie Ames Byrd (d. 1974); he named Marie Byrd Land and the Ames Range after her and her father, respectively. They had four children: Richard Evelyn Byrd III, Evelyn Bolling Byrd Clarke, Katharine Agnes Byrd Breyer, and Helen Byrd Stabler. The family moved to a brownstone at 9 Brimmer Street in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood in late 1924, purchased by Marie’s father, a wealthy industrialist. Byrd was friends with Edsel Ford and Henry Ford, whose admiration for his polar exploits helped secure Ford Motor Company sponsorship for his expeditions. He owned a pet dog named Igloo, who accompanied him to both poles and is buried at the Pine Ridge Pet Cemetery with a tombstone reading "He was more than a friend." Byrd attended the Virginia Military Institute for two years, transferred to the University of Virginia, and then entered the United States Naval Academy on May 28, 1908. He graduated on June 8, 1912, as an ensign and was assigned to the USS Wyoming; during service in the Caribbean, he received a letter of commendation and a Silver Lifesaving Medal for rescuing sailors twice by diving fully clothed. In April 1914, he transferred to the USS Washington and served in Mexican waters. He later served on the USS Dolphin, which also served as the yacht of the Secretary of the Navy, where he met future Fleet Admiral William D. Leahy and Assistant Secretary of the Navy Franklin Roosevelt. He was promoted to lieutenant (junior grade) on June 8, 1915. His last assignment before forced retirement was on the presidential yacht USS Mayflower. On March 15, 1916, he was medically retired on three-quarters pay due to an ankle injury sustained on the Mayflower. He was then assigned as inspector and instructor for the Rhode Island Naval Militia, where he was commended by Brigadier General Charles W. Abbot for improving its efficiency. After the U.S. entered World War I in April 1917, Byrd oversaw the mobilization of the Rhode Island Naval Militia and was recalled to active duty, serving in the Office of Naval Operations as secretary and organizer of the Navy Department Commission on Training Camps. In the autumn of 1917, he attended naval aviation school at Pensacola, Florida, and qualified as a naval aviator (number 608) in June 1918. He commanded naval air forces at Naval Air Station Halifax, Canada, from July 1918 until the armistice in November, during which he was promoted to the permanent rank of lieutenant and the temporary rank of lieutenant commander. For his wartime service, he received a letter of commendation from Secretary of the Navy Josephus Daniels, later converted to a Navy Commendation Medal. After the war, Byrd volunteered for the U.S. Navy’s 1919 aerial transatlantic crossing, the first time the Atlantic was flown across by aircraft. Though his service in Newfoundland was considered overseas, he contributed by planning the flight path. Only Lieutenant Commander Albert Read’s NC-4 completed the flight on May 18, 1919. In 1921, Byrd attempted a solo nonstop Atlantic crossing, six years before Charles Lindbergh, but was denied due to concerns over risk by acting Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt Jr. He was then assigned to the ill-fated dirigible ZR-2 (formerly the British R-38), which broke apart in midair on August 24, 1921, killing 44 of 49 crew members. Byrd lost friends in the accident and participated in recovery and investigation, an event that deeply affected him and led him to prioritize safety in future expeditions. Due to postwar Navy reductions, Byrd reverted to the rank of lieutenant in 1921. In summer 1923, he and other World War I Navy veterans founded the Naval Reserve Air Station (NRAS) at Squantum Point near Boston, using an unused seaplane hangar, which was commissioned on August 15, 1923, and is considered the first air base in the Naval Reserve program. From June to October 1925, Byrd commanded the aviation unit of an arctic expedition to North Greenland led by Donald B. MacMillan, though the expedition did not reach the pole. Byrd’s aviation contributions, however, earned him recognition as a pioneer of aircraft in exploration. During this expedition, he met Navy Chief Aviation Pilot Floyd Bennett and Norwegian pilot Bernt Balchen, both of whom later contributed to his expeditions. Bennett piloted Byrd’s 1926 North Pole flight, and Balchen became the primary pilot on the 1929 South Pole flight. On May 9, 1926, Byrd and Bennett flew a Fokker F.VIIa/3m tri-motor monoplane named Josephine Ford from Spitsbergen (Svalbard) to the North Pole and back, lasting 15 hours and 57 minutes, including 13 minutes circling at their farthest north, covering a distance of 1,535 miles (1,335 nautical miles). Upon returning to the U.S., Byrd became a national hero, was paraded in New York City, and on December 21, 1926, Congress promoted him to commander and awarded both him and Bennett the Medal of Honor. The Josephine Ford was flown across the country in celebration, and Bennett was promoted to warrant officer rank of machinist. Byrd and Bennett received Tiffany Cross versions of the Medal of Honor on March 5, 1927, at the White House from President Calvin Coolidge. Since 1926, doubts have arisen about whether Byrd actually reached the North Pole. In 1958, Bernt Balchen questioned Byrd’s claim, stating that Bennett had confessed months later that they had not reached the pole. Bennett, who had not fully recovered from a prior crash, died of pneumonia in April 1928 after participating in a rescue flight. However, Bennett had written memoirs, given interviews, and published an article confirming Byrd’s account before his death. The 1996 release of Byrd’s diary revealed erased sextant sights that differ from his later official report: at 7:07:10 GCT, his diary shows a solar altitude of 19°25'30", while his official report states 18°18'18". Dennis Rawlins concluded that Byrd flew about 80% of the distance to the pole before turning back due to an engine oil leak and later falsified his official report to claim reaching the pole. A defender of Byrd suggests a westerly-moving anticyclone provided tailwinds that boosted ground speed, allowing the claimed distance to be covered in the stated time, though this theory is challenged by Rawlins, who notes that the precision of the sextant data in the official typewritten report (to 1 second) is not feasible for 1926 Navy sextants, unlike the more accurate data in Byrd’s diary. If Byrd and Bennett did not reach the North Pole, the first flight over the pole occurred on May 12, 1926, when the airship Norge, piloted by Roald Amundsen, Umberto Nobile, Oscar Wisting, and Lincoln Ellsworth, flew from Spitsbergen to Alaska. In 1927, Byrd announced support from the American Trans-Oceanic Company, established in 1914 by Rodman Wanamaker, to attempt the first nonstop transatlantic flight. He named Floyd Bennett as chief pilot, with Bernt Balchen, Bert Acosta, and Lieutenant George Noville as crew. During a practice takeoff, the Fokker Trimotor America crashed, severely injuring Bennett and slightly injuring Byrd. Charles Lindbergh won the Orteig Prize on May 21, 1927, completing the first nonstop transatlantic flight. Byrd then named Balchen as chief pilot to replace Bennett. On June 29, 1927, Byrd, Balchen, Acosta, and Noville flew the America from Roosevelt Field, New York, to France, arriving the next day but being prevented from landing in Paris due to cloud cover. They crash-landed near Ver-sur-Mer (Gold Beach) on July 1, 1927, without fatalities. In France, Byrd and his crew were received as heroes and Byrd was invested as an Officer of the French Legion of Honor by Prime Minister Raymond Poincaré on July 6. After returning to the U.S., an elaborate dinner was held in New York City on July 19, where Byrd and Noville were awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross by Secretary of the Navy Curtis D. Wilbur; Acosta and Balchen were not awarded due to the Distinguished Flying Cross being limited to military personnel at the time. Byrd wrote an article for the August 1927 edition of Popular Science Monthly, accurately predicting that specially modified aircraft with one to three crewmen could fly the Atlantic nonstop, though commercial realization would take another 20 years. In 1928, Byrd began his first Antarctic expedition with two ships—the City of New York (formerly Samson, noted for being near the Titanic) and the Eleanor Bolling (named after his mother)—and three aircraft: a Ford Trimotor named Floyd Bennett (after Bennett), a Fairchild FC-2W2 named Stars And Stripes (now at the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center), and a Fokker Super Universal named Virginia (named after his birth state). A base camp named "Little America" was established on the Ross Ice Shelf, and scientific expeditions using snowshoes, dog sleds, snowmobiles, and airplanes began. A 19-year-old Boy Scout, Paul Allman Siple, was selected to join, later earning a doctorate and participating in all five of Byrd’s Antarctic expeditions. Photographic expeditions and geological surveys were conducted, and constant radio communication was maintained. After their first winter, expeditions resumed, and on November 28, 1929, the first flight to the South Pole and back was launched. Byrd, with pilot Bernt Balchen, co-pilot/radioman Harold June, and photographer Ashley McKinley, flew the Floyd Bennett to the South Pole and back in 18 hours and 41 minutes. They struggled to gain altitude and had to dump empty gas tanks and emergency supplies to reach the Antarctic Plateau, but ultimately succeeded. In November 1929, Byrd led a privately financed expedition where his aircraft crew successfully flew over the South Pole. He strongly advocated for ski-equipped aircraft, despite significant operational, logistical, and maintenance challenges, which required the establishment of substantial onshore bases. As a result of this achievement, Byrd was promoted to the next rank.

Other than Byrd himself, no one else participated in all five of Byrd's Antarctic expeditions. During the summer of 1929, photographic expeditions and geological surveys were conducted, with constant radio communications maintained with the outside world. After their first winter, the expedition resumed, and on November 28, 1929, the first flight to the South Pole and back was launched by Byrd, pilot Bernt Balchen, co-pilot/radioman Harold June, and photographer Ashley McKinley, who flew the Floyd Bennett to the South Pole and back in 18 hours, 41 minutes. They struggled to gain sufficient altitude and had to dump empty gas tanks and emergency supplies to reach the Antarctic Plateau, but ultimately succeeded. In November 1929, Byrd led a privately financed expedition that successfully flew over the South Pole, strongly advocating for ski-equipped aircraft despite significant operational, logistical, and maintenance challenges that required large onshore bases. As a result, Byrd was promoted to rear admiral by special act of Congress on December 21, 1929, becoming the youngest admiral in U.S. Navy history at age 41; none of his Annapolis classmates became admirals until 1942 after 30 years of service. He is one of only four persons, including Admiral David Dixon Porter, Rear Admiral Donald Baxter MacMillan, and Rear Admiral Frederic R. Harris, to have been promoted to rear admiral without first holding the rank of captain. The expedition returned to North America on June 18, 1930, and was honored with the gold medal of the American Geographical Society; it was also featured in the film With Byrd at the South Pole (1930). Byrd, now an internationally recognized polar explorer and aviator, served as Honorary National President of Pi Gamma Mu (1931–1935), carrying the society's flag during his first Antarctic expedition to highlight the spirit of adventure in both natural and social sciences. To secure political and public support, Byrd cultivated relationships with powerful individuals such as President Franklin Roosevelt, Henry Ford, Edsel Ford, John D. Rockefeller Jr., and Vincent Astor, naming geographic features in Antarctica after them. During his second expedition (1933–1934), winter in the Northern Hemisphere, Byrd spent five months alone at Advance Base, narrowly escaping death from carbon monoxide poisoning due to a poorly ventilated stove. Unusual radio transmissions alarmed base camp personnel, who attempted to reach him; the first two trips failed due to darkness, snow, and mechanical issues. Thomas Poulter, E. J. Demas, and Amory Waite eventually reached Advance Base, where they found Byrd in poor health; they remained until October 12, when an airplane picked up Dr. Poulter and Byrd, and the rest returned with a tractor. This experience is detailed in Byrd’s autobiography Alone. During the summer, days were long with twilight evenings, and Byrd maintained a large calendar in the headquarters to track each day. A CBS radio station, KFZ, was established on the base camp ship, the Bear of Oakland, and the program The Adventures of Admiral Byrd was broadcast via shortwave to Buenos Aires and then to New York. Sponsored by General Foods, it aired on Saturday nights at 10:00 pm and reached #16 on the Hooper rating for the 1933–34 season with an average audience of 19.1 million. President Roosevelt and the U.S. Postmaster General honored the expedition in 1933 with a U.S. commemorative stamp, which helped fund the mission. The stamp, numbered 753 in Scott’s Catalog, required a 3-cent Byrd II stamp and 53 cents in additional postage for mail to Antarctica, which was processed through a special U.S. Post Office established at Little America on October 6, 1933. Approximately 150,000 pieces of mail passed through the post office between 1933 and 1934. Only authorized post office personnel could handle mail, and Charles F. Anderson, a special representative of the Postmaster General, was assigned to Little America. In late 1938, Byrd visited Hamburg to present his Antarctic film to members of the German Antarctic Expedition 1938/39, answering questions and offering practical advice based on his polar experience in a private event with no press. Byrd's third expedition was the first U.S. government-financed one, including studies in geology, biology, meteorology, and exploration, and featured the innovative Antarctic Snow Cruiser, which broke down shortly after arrival. By March 1940, Byrd was recalled to active duty in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations; the expedition continued until its last participants left on March 22, 1941. In March 1942, Byrd was recalled again and served as confidential advisor to Admiral Ernest J. King, participating in the South Pacific Island Base Inspection Board from 1942 to 1945, which toured South Pacific bases in May and June 1942 and submitted a report analyzing base conditions and offering recommendations for future planning. On September 1, 1943, Byrd was ordered to lead a survey of East and South Pacific islands related to national defense and commercial air bases and routes. The Special Navy Mission sailed from Balboa on USS Concord, commanded by Captain Irving Reynold Chambers, in September 1943. On October 7, 1943, a large explosion at sea, caused by gasoline fumes at the stern, killed 24 crewmen, including executive officer Commander Rogers Elliott, and injured others; some were thrown overboard or killed by concussion, burns, or broken bones. The dead were buried at sea on October 8. On October 23, 1943, Byrd wrote to Chambers commending his crew for "courage and efficiency," expressing pride in their heroism. Byrd completed the mission in December and participated in the United States Strategic Bombing Survey (USSBS) from 1944 to 1945. On February 10, 1945, Byrd received the Order of Christopher Columbus from the Dominican Republic. He was present at the Japanese surrender in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, and was released from active duty on October 1, 1945. For his World War II service, he received two awards of the Legion of Merit. In 1946, Secretary of the Navy James Forrestal appointed Byrd as officer in charge of the Antarctic Developments Project. His fourth expedition, Operation Highjump, was the largest to date and was expected to last 6–8 months. It was supported by a large naval force (Task Force 68), including 13 U.S. Navy support ships (besides the flagship USS Mount Olympus and aircraft carrier USS Philippine Sea), six helicopters, six flying boats, two seaplane tenders, and 15 other aircraft, involving over 4,000 personnel. The armada arrived in the Ross Sea on December 31, 1946, and conducted aerial explorations of an area half the size of the United States, recording 10 new mountain ranges, primarily along the eastern coastline of Antarctica from 150°E to the Greenwich meridian. In an interview with Lee van Atta of International News Service aboard the USS Mount Olympus, Byrd warned that the U.S. should prepare for attacks by hostile planes from polar regions, stating that the shrinking world meant isolation was no longer a guarantee of safety. The interview appeared in the March 5, 1947, edition of Chilean newspaper El Mercurio. In 1948, the U.S. Navy produced The Secret Land, a documentary about Operation Highjump that won the Academy Award for Best Documentary. On December 8, 1954, Byrd appeared on Longines Chronoscope, where he discussed his Antarctic voyages and stated that Antarctica would become the most important scientific location in the world. As part of the International Geophysical Year (1957–58), Byrd was appointed officer in charge of U.S. Navy Operation Deep Freeze I in 1955–56, which established permanent bases at McMurdo Sound, the Bay of Whales, and the South Pole—marking the beginning of a permanent U.S. military presence in Antarctica. Byrd spent only one week in Antarctica and began his return to the U.S. on February 3, 1956. He died in his sleep of a heart ailment at age 68 on March 11, 1957, at his home in Boston’s Beacon Hill neighborhood and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Byrd was an active Freemason, raised in Federal Lodge No. 1, Washington, D.C., on March 19, 1921, and affiliated with Kane Lodge No. 454, New York City, on September 18, 1928, and was a member of National Sojourners Chapter No. 3 at Washington. In 1930, he received a gold medal from Kane Lodge. In 1931, Byrd became a compatriot of the Tennessee Society of the Sons of the American Revolution, receiving state membership number 605 and national number 50430, and was awarded the War Service Medal for First World War service. He was also a member of the Explorers Club, American Legion, and National Geographic Society. By the time of his death, Byrd had 22 citations and special commendations, nine for bravery and two for extraordinary heroism in saving lives; he also received the Medal of Honor, Silver Lifesaving Medal, Navy Distinguished Service Medal, Distinguished Flying Cross, and Navy Cross. He is the only person to have three ticker-tape parades in New York City (1926, 1927, 1930). He was one of only four American military officers entitled to wear a medal with his own image, including Admiral George Dewey, General John J. Pershing, and Admiral William T. Sampson; Byrd’s image appears on both the first and second Byrd Antarctic Expedition Medals, making him the only American to wear two such medals. He received the Langley Gold Medal from the Smithsonian Institution and was the seventh recipient of the Hubbard Medal from the National Geographic Society for his North Pole flight, alongside Robert Peary, Roald Amundsen, and Charles Lindbergh. He also received the David Livingstone Centenary Medal, Loczy Medal, Vega Medal, and Elisha Kent Kane Medal from various geographical societies. In 1927, the Boy Scouts of America made Byrd an Honorary Scout, a new category created that year for citizens whose achievements in exploration and adventure inspired boys. In 1927, the City of Richmond dedicated the Richard Evelyn Byrd Flying Field, now Richmond International Airport, in Henrico County, Virginia; Byrd's Fairchild FC-2W2, NX8006, Stars And Stripes, is on display at the Virginia Aviation Museum. In 1929, Byrd received the Silver Buffalo Award and the Langley Gold Medal. Lunar crater Byrd, the U.S. Navy dry cargo ship USNS Richard E. Byrd (T-AKE-4), and the decommissioned guided missile destroyer USS Richard E. Byrd (DDG-23) are named after him. In 1930, Byrd was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In Glen Rock, New Jersey, the Richard E. Byrd School was dedicated in 1931. On March 31, 1934, during a scheduled broadcast, Byrd was awarded the CBS Medal for Distinguished Contribution to Radio, recognizing his short-wave relay broadcasts from the second expedition as a milestone in communication history; he was the sixth recipient. The Institute of Polar Studies at Ohio State University changed its name to the Byrd Polar Research Center (BPRC) on January 21, 1987, after acquiring Byrd’s expedition records, personal papers, and memorabilia from Marie A. Byrd’s estate in 1985; his papers formed the nucleus of the BPRC Polar Archival Program in 1990. In 1958, the Richard Byrd Library opened in Springfield, Virginia, as part of the Fairfax County Public Library system. Richard E. Byrd Elementary School in Negishi, Yokohama, Japan, opened on September 20, 1948, and was renamed R.E. Byrd Elementary School on April 5, 1960. Memorials to Byrd exist in Wellington and Dunedin, New Zealand, which served as his departure point for several expeditions. In 1979, the Australian Antarctic Territory issued a set of two postage stamps commemorating the 50th anniversary of Byrd’s first flight over the South Pole, along with a commemorative flag. The long-range short-wave voice transmissions from Byrd’s 1934 expedition were named an IEEE Milestone in 2001.

Admiral Richard E. Byrd, born October 25, 1888, in Winchester, Virginia, and appointed from Virginia, was a Commander in the United States Navy and one of the most highly decorated officers in U.S. Navy history. He is probably the only individual to have received the Medal of Honor, Navy Cross, Distinguished Flying Cross, and the Silver Life Saving Medal, and one of only a few to have earned all three Antarctic expedition medals issued before World War II. Byrd was awarded the Medal of Honor by President Calvin Coolidge on March 5, 1927, for courage and intrepidity in demonstrating that aircraft could fly continuously from a populated area over the North Pole and return, alongside Machinist Floyd Bennett. The Navy Cross was awarded in 1929 for leading the flight to the South Pole on November 29, 1929, from Little America, Antarctica, under extreme cold and high-altitude conditions, with a forced landing being beyond probable rescue. In 1926, he received a Gold Star in lieu of a second Navy Distinguished Service Medal for organizing the U.S. Antarctic Service, establishing two bases 1,500 miles apart, and conducting significant explorations, including four flights that discovered new mountain ranges, islands, over 100,000 square miles of land, a peninsula, and 700 miles of previously unknown Antarctic coast. He also earned the Legion of Merit in 1943 for surveying thirty-three Pacific islands for air base sites and a second Gold Star in lieu of a second Legion of Merit from 1942 to 1945 for his role as a confidential advisor to the Commander in Chief, United States Fleet, providing strategic counsel that contributed to the war effort. He received the Distinguished Flying Cross in 1927 for flying the "America" from New York to France under adverse weather, landing safely at Ver sur Mer after 39 hours and 56 minutes. Byrd was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa as an honorary member at the University of Virginia and into the International Air and Space Hall of Fame in 1968. His papers, including 985 documents from the estate of Marie A. Byrd, the late wife of Admiral Byrd, formed the foundation of the BPRC Polar Archival Program in 1990. The Richard Byrd Library, part of the Fairfax County Public Library system, opened in Springfield, Virginia, in 1958. Richard E. Byrd Elementary School in Negishi, Yokohama, Japan, opened on September 20, 1948, and was renamed R.E. Byrd Elementary School on April 5, 1960. Admiral Byrd Middle School in Frederick County, Virginia, opened in 2005 and is decorated with images and letters from his life and career. A school in Sun Valley, California, named Richard E. Byrd Middle School, opened in its current location in 2008 after its original site became Sun Valley High School. Memorials to Byrd are located in Wellington and Dunedin, New Zealand, where he used the country as a departure point for several Antarctic expeditions. The 50th anniversary of his first flight over the South Pole was commemorated in 1979 by Australian Antarctic Territory with a set of two postage stamps and a commemorative flag. Long-range short-wave voice transmissions from his 1934 Antarctic expedition were named an IEEE Milestone in 2001. Byrd was posthumously eligible for the Antarctic Service Medal, established in 1960, for his participation in Operation Highjump (1946–1947) and Operation Deep Freeze (1955–1956). He also received numerous other awards from U.S. governmental and private entities. In Great Circle by Maggie Shipstead, Byrd and the Little America bases are the final stop in Marian Graves' journey to circle the globe by flight over the North and South Poles. Jacques Vallée, in his book Confrontations, references a "spurious story" about "holes in the pole" allegedly found by Byrd, citing Clint Chapin of the Copper Medic case as believing UFOs originated from within the Earth.
